blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Gravitation :- Gravitation is a phenomena in which objects with masses have a natural tendency to attract each other.

Newton's Law of Gravitation :-

$F_g = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$

  • This formula is given for point masses. For spherical objects (planets), distance between centers is taken.
$G$ = Universal Gravitational constant

Value of G :

SI : G = 6.67 × 10–11 N–m2/kg2

CGS : G = 6.67 × 10–8 dyne–cm2/g2

Dimensions : [M–1L3T–2]

Forces due to multiple particles :-

$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 + \vec{F}_3 + \cdots$$$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: A small object of mass m rotates about a very large and heavy object of mass M with constant speed V0. Then find the radius of its circular path R.
blocks.answer:
$F_g = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$

Here for circular motion of particle, necessary centripetal force is provided by gravitation force.

$F_g = F_{\text{CP}}$

$F_{\text{CP}} = \frac{m v_0^2}{R}$

$\frac{GMm}{R^2}$=$\frac{m v_0^2}{R}$

$R = \frac{GM}{v_0^2}$
blocks.prompt: A small object of mass m rotates about a very large and heavy object of mass M with constant speed V0. Then find the radius of its circular path R.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text: Misunderstanding the Concept of r: Misinterpret the value of r (the distance between the centers of the two masses) by not accounting for the radii of the objects involved.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Gravitational field :- It is the region around a mass where its gravitational effects can be observed.

(1) At infinity gravitational field is zero.
(2) Gravitational field $\propto$ mass

• Gravitational field is conservative in nature.

There are two ways to measure the strength of the gravitational field.

(1) Gravitational field intensity.
(2) Gravitational potential

Gravitational field intensity $(\vec{I})$ :- It is defined as gravitational force exerted on a unit mass placed in a gravitational field.

$\vec{I}$=$\frac{F}{m}$

• It is a vector quantity.
    • Its direction is same as that of gravitational force.
    • Unit :- N/kg

• Dimension :- [MoL1T–2]
    • Force on a particle of mass 'm' placed in gravitational field having intensity can be written as –

$\vec{F}=m\vec{I}$

Gravitational field intensity due to a point mass :-

$\vec{I}$=$\frac{GM}{r^2}$$(-\hat{r})$

  • Negative sign indicates that the force due to gravitational field is attractive in nature.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ignoring the Direction: Always consider the direction of the gravitational field, which is towards the mass causing the field.
  • Incorrect Application of Superposition Principle: Ensure vector addition is used when calculating net gravitational fields from multiple sources.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Acceleration due to gravity : If a body is placed inside a gravitational field having intensity I, gravitational force applied on it .

$F=mI$

Earth also pulls every object towards its center with force.

$F=mg$

$g=$$|\vec{I}|$

Where, $g$ is acceleration due to gravity $I$ Is intensity of gravitational field due to Earth

Variation in acceleration due to gravity with height :

$g_h=\dfrac{g}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R_e}\right)^2}$

Special case :- If h <<<< ${R}$ ( $h \leqslant 320\,km$ )

$g_h = g \left( 1 - \frac{2h}{R_e} \right)$

Variation in acceleration due to gravity with depth 'd' :

$g_d = g_s \left( 1 - \frac{d}{R} \right)$

Note : Valid for large and small depth

Variation of $g$ :

Variation in value of 'g' due to rotation of earth :

$g_{\text{eff}} = g - \omega^2 R_e \cos^2(\lambda)$

$\lambda$ = Angle of latitude

For Poles ,$\lambda = 90^\circ$

For Equator,$\lambda = 0^\circ$

$N = Mg - M\omega^2 R_e \cos^2(\lambda)$

Note: As one moves towards pole, apparent weight increases.

• If the earth suddenly stops rotating about its own axis, then apparent weight of bodies or effective acceleration due to gravity will increase at all the places except poles.
Variation in value of "g" due to shape of Earth:

Radius of earth at poles is lesser than radius of earth at equator.

${R_p} < {R_e}$ , so

$\mathbf{g}_p > \mathbf{g}_{eq}$

  • Incorrect Sign Convention
  • Assuming g is Always 9.8 m/s² Everywhere

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Gravitational Field Intensity (E) :-

$\vec{I}$=$\frac{F}{m}$

  • Units: $\text{N/kg}$ or $\text{m/s}^2$
  • Gravitational Field intensity due to multiple particles
  • $\vec{I}_{\text{net}} = \vec{I}_1 + \vec{I}_2 + \vec{I}_3 + \cdots$
  • Neutral point: A point in space, Where Inet = 0.For two particle system, Neutral point exists on the line joining of the particles.
Neutral Point-Neutral point is closer to the lighter particle.

Gravitational field Intensity due to spheres :-

(1) For solid sphere

Case(1) When  $r>R$ (Outside the sphere)

$\vec{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{out}}$=$\frac{GM}{r^2}$$(-\hat{r})$

Case(2) When  $r=R$ at the surface

$\vec{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{surface}}$=$\frac{GM}{R^2}$$(-\hat{r})$

(3) When $r<R$ inside the sphere

$\vec{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{in}}$=$\frac{GM r}{R^3}$$(-\hat{r})$

Variation of $I$ with  $r$ :-

$I_{\text{max}} = I_{\text{surface}} = \frac{GM}{R^2}$

$I_{\text{min}} = I_{\text{centre}} = \frac{GM}{R^3}$$(0)$$=0$

Gravitational field intensity due to a hollow sphere :-

Case(1) When  $r>R$ (Outside the shell)

$\vec{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{out}}$=$\frac{GM}{r^2}$$(-\hat{r})$

Case(2) When  $r=R$ at the surface

$\vec{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{surface}}$=$\frac{GM}{R^2}$$(-\hat{r})$

Case(3) When $r<R$ inside the shell then $I=0$

Variation of $I$ with $r$ :-

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Gravitational potential due to point mass$(V)$ :-

$V = \frac{W_{\text{ext}}}{m}$

$V = -\frac{GM}{r}$

Relation between Potential and Intensity :-

$\mathrm{I}=-\frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dr}}$

  • If V is constant in a region, $I$= 0
  • This relation is valid for all conservative fields

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
Spherical shell (M, R) :-

Case (1): $\mathrm{r>R}$ (outside the sphere)

$\mathrm{V_{\text {out }}=-\frac{G M}{r}}$

Case(2): $r=R(\text { on the surface }) ; V_{\text {surfiace }}=-\frac{G M}{R}$

Case (3): r < R (inside the sphere ; Potential is same every where and is

equal to its value at the surface$V_{\text {in }}=-\frac{G M}{R}$

Solid sphere(M, R) :-

Case (1) : $\mathrm{r>R}$ (outside the sphere)

$\mathrm{V_{\text {out }}=-\frac{G M}{r}}$

Case(2) : $\mathrm{r=R}$ (on the surface)

$\mathrm{V_{surface}=-\frac{G M}{R}}$

Case (3) : $\mathrm{r<R}$ (inside the sphere)

$\mathrm{V_{i n}=-\frac{G M}{2 R^3}\left(3 R^2-r^2\right)}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing gravitational potential with gravitational potential energy.
  • Forgetting the negative sign in potential and potential energy.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
The gravitational potential energy of a particle situated at a point in some gravitational field is defined as the amount of work required to bring it from infinity to that point without changing its kinetic energy.

$\mathrm{U}=-\frac{\mathrm{Gm}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2}{\mathrm{r}}$

(Here negative sign shows the boundness of the two bodies)

The gravitational potential energy of a particle of mass 'm' placed on the surface of earth of mass 'M' and radius 'R' is given by :

$\mathrm{U}=-\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}}$

Gravitational potential energy for three particle system :-

$\mathrm{U}_{\text {system }}=$ $\mathrm{-\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r_1}-\frac{G m_2 m_3}{r_2}-\frac{G m_1 m_3}{r_3}}$

If Gravitational Potential at a point P is $V_{\text{P}}$, then GPE of a particle of mass m placed at P is :

$\mathrm{U_P=m\left(V_P\right)}$

At Infinity

$V_{\infty} = 0 \quad U_{\infty} = 0$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: Find gravitational potential energy of a particle of mass "m" placed at a height R. above surface of solid sphere of mass "M" and Radius "R".
blocks.answer:
$V = -\frac{GM}{r}$

$V = -\frac{GM}{(R + h)}$$=-\frac{GM}{(R + R)}$=$-\frac{GM}{2R}$

Now potential energy (U) = V(m)

$U = -\frac{GM}{2R}(m)$

$U = -\frac{GM}{2R}m$
blocks.prompt: Find gravitational potential energy of a particle of mass "m" placed at a height R. above surface of solid sphere of mass "M" and Radius "R".

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Using the Wrong Reference Point
  • Assuming Zero Potential Energy for Objects at Ground Level
  • Confusing Work-Energy Theorem with Potential Energy

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Escape velocity :- Minimum speed given to a body due to a which the body escapes from planet's gravitational field is called escape velocity. It does not depend on the direction of throw.

The escape velocity of a body from a location which is at height 'h' above the surface of body,

$\mathrm{v_e=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R+h}} \quad\{\because r=R+h\}}$

Escape speed depends on :-

(1) Mass (M) and radius (R) of the planet

(2) Position from where the particle is projected.

Escape speed does not depend on :-

(i) Mass (m) of the body which is projected

(ii) Angle of projection.

For Earth :-

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}}}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
Escape velocity from a point other than surface :-

1. Total energy is zero at any point when particle start moving with escape velocity, T.E. = 0

2. If given point is at distance $\mathrm{r(>R)}$ from center of Earth,

$\mathrm{PE}_{\text {out }}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}_e \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{r}}$

3. If given point is at distance $\mathrm{r(<R)}$ from center of Earth,

$\mathrm{PE}_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}\left(3 \mathrm{R}^2-\mathrm{r}^2\right)}{2 \mathrm{R}^3} \times \mathrm{m}$

Escape energy :- Minimum energy given to a particle in the form of kinetic energy so that it can just escape the Earth's gravitational field.

Escape energy = Kinetic Energy corresponding to the escape velocity $\Rightarrow$$\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{e}}^2$

Note:

(1) KE < Escape Energy   $\mathrm{v_o<v_e} \Rightarrow$ Body returns to Earth surface

(2) KE = Escape Energy   $\mathrm{v_o=v_e}  \Rightarrow$ Body comes to rest at infinity

(3) KE > Escape Energy    $\mathrm{v_o>v_e}  \Rightarrow$ Body has residual velocity at infinity

blocks.title: Example- 1
blocks.question: An unknown planet is of twice the size and half the mass of Earth. If escape velocity from Earth surface is Vo, what would be escape velocity of particle from the unknown planet.
blocks.prompt: An unknown planet is of twice the size and half the mass of Earth. If escape velocity from Earth surface is Vo, what would be escape velocity of particle from the unknown planet.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A narrow tunnel is dug along the diameter of the earth (Me, R), and a particle of mass 'm' is placed at 'R/2' distance from the centre. Find the escape speed of the particle from that place.
blocks.answer:
suppose we project the particle with speed $v_e$

So that it just reaches infinity ($r \to \infty$)

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$\frac{1}{2} m v_e^2 + M \left[ -\frac{GM_e}{2R^3} \left( 3R^2 - \left( \frac{R}{2} \right)^2 \right) \right] = 0$

$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{11GM_e}{4R}}$

modules.name: Satellite Motion and Types of Satellite

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Satellite :- A light body revolving round a heavier planet due to gravitational attraction, is called a satellite. Moon is a natural satellite of Earth.

Essential conditions for satellite motion :-

• The centre of satellite's orbit should coincide with the centre of Earth.
    • Plane of the orbit of satellite should pass through the centre of Earth.

There are two stable orbits for a satellite

• Equatorial orbit

• Polar orbit

Any satellite is projected as near to equator as possible as-

• g is minimum near equator, lesser fuel consumption

• Easier to set the satellite in any orbit

Geostationary Satellite:- A geostationary satellite appears stationary in the sky from a specific point on Earth's surface because its orbital period matches the Earth's rotation period of 24 hours. It orbits at an altitude of approximately 35,786 kilometers (22,236 miles) above the equator. This orbit is known as a geostationary orbit.

Polar satellite:- It  is a type of Earth-observing satellite that orbits the Earth, passing over or near the Earth's poles.

• It rotates in Polar plane.

• Its height from Earth surface is 500 km ~ 600 km.

• Its time period is 100 min.

• Used for weather data collection

Note: Any satellite is said to be in a condition of freely falling on Earth. (as only force acting on it is force

of gravity). Hence, apparent weight of any object in a satellite is always ZERO.

Orbital Velocity ($v_0$) :-

$\mathrm{v_0=\sqrt{\frac{GM_e}{r}}}$

Time period of orbital motion :-

$\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{r}}}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~T}^2 \propto \mathrm{r}^3$

Kinetic energy of satellite :-

$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{r}}$

Potential energy of satellite :-

$\mathrm{PE}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{r}}$

Total Mechanical Energy ($\mathrm{TE}$) :-

$\mathrm{TE}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{r}}$

$\mathrm{KE}=-\mathrm{TE}=-\frac{\mathrm{PE}}{2}$

As total energy of a satellite is negative, it is called as bounded system.

Binding energy (BE = –TE)

$\mathrm{BE}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{r}}$

Work done to shift orbit of satellite :-

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {ext }}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)$

blocks.question: Satellites A and B are orbiting around the Earth in orbits of radius ratio 1 : 4, find ratio of their orbital velocities.
blocks.prompt: Satellites A and B are orbiting around the Earth in orbits of radius ratio 1 : 4, find ratio of their orbital velocities.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Assuming the gravitational force is constant for all satellite orbits.
  • Confusing the formula for circular orbits with elliptical orbits.
  • Confusing the concept of geostationary orbits with other types of orbits.
  • Using Kepler’s Third Law without accounting for the masses of both the orbiting body and the central body.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Kepler's 1st Law :-  Each planet moves in an elliptical orbit, with the sun at one focus of the ellipse.

Kepler's 2nd law (Law of Areas) :- A line joining any planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, i.e. the areal velocity of the planet remains constant.

$r \times v=\text { constant }$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{P}}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{A}}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{r}_{\min }}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{max}}}$

$\displaystyle a = \frac{r_{\text{max}} + r_{\text{min}}}{2}$

Note:

• At minimum distance from Sun, velocity is maximum.

• At maximum distance from Sun, velocity is minimum.

Kepler's 3rd law :- The square of the period of revolution of any planet around the Sun is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit.

$T^2 \propto a^3$

$a = \frac{r_{\text{max}} + r_{\text{min}}}{2}$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: A small satellite is in an elliptical orbit around the Earth, as shown in the figure. If L is its angular momentum with respect to the center of the Earth and K is its kinetic energy, then compare the kinetic energy of the satellite at positions 1 and 2
blocks.answer:
Since the torque of the gravitational attraction with respect to the Sun is zero, the angular momentum of the planet with respect to the Sun remains constant.

$\mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{mv}_1 \mathrm{r}_1=\mathrm{mv}_2 \mathrm{r}_2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}_1 \mathrm{r}_1=\mathrm{v}_2 \mathrm{r}_2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}_1>\mathrm{r}_2$

$\mathrm{v}_1=\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_2 \mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}$

$\begin{aligned} & v_2>v_1 \\ & \frac{1}{2} m v_2^2>\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2 \Rightarrow K_2>K_1 \end{aligned}$

Escape velocity :- Minimum speed given to a body due to a which the body escapes from planet's gravitational field is called escape velocity. It does not depend on the direction of throw.

The escape velocity of a body from a location which is at height 'h' above the surface of body,

$\mathrm{v_e=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R+h}} \quad\{\because r=R+h\}}$

Escape speed depends on :-

(1) Mass (M) and radius (R) of the planet

(2) Position from where the particle is projected.

Escape speed does not depend on :-

(i) Mass (m) of the body which is projected

(ii) Angle of projection.

For Earth :-

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}}}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
Escape velocity from a point other than surface :-

1. Total energy is zero at any point when particle start moving with escape velocity, T.E. = 0

2. If given point is at distance $\mathrm{r(>R)}$ from center of Earth,

$\mathrm{PE}_{\text {out }}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}_e \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{r}}$

3. If given point is at distance $\mathrm{r(<R)}$ from center of Earth,

$\mathrm{PE}_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}\left(3 \mathrm{R}^2-\mathrm{r}^2\right)}{2 \mathrm{R}^3} \times \mathrm{m}$

Escape energy :- Minimum energy given to a particle in the form of kinetic energy so that it can just escape the Earth's gravitational field.

Escape energy = Kinetic Energy corresponding to the escape velocity $\Rightarrow$$\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{e}}^2$

Note:

(1) KE < Escape Energy   $\mathrm{v_o<v_e} \Rightarrow$ Body returns to Earth surface

(2) KE = Escape Energy   $\mathrm{v_o=v_e}  \Rightarrow$ Body comes to rest at infinity

(3) KE > Escape Energy    $\mathrm{v_o>v_e}  \Rightarrow$ Body has residual velocity at infinity

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Satellite :- A light body revolving round a heavier planet due to gravitational attraction, is called a satellite. Moon is a natural satellite of Earth.

Essential conditions for satellite motion :-

• The centre of satellite's orbit should coincide with the centre of Earth.
    • Plane of the orbit of satellite should pass through the centre of Earth.

There are two stable orbits for a satellite

• Equatorial orbit

• Polar orbit

Any satellite is projected as near to equator as possible as-

• g is minimum near equator, lesser fuel consumption

• Easier to set the satellite in any orbit

Geostationary Satellite:- A geostationary satellite appears stationary in the sky from a specific point on Earth's surface because its orbital period matches the Earth's rotation period of 24 hours. It orbits at an altitude of approximately 35,786 kilometers (22,236 miles) above the equator. This orbit is known as a geostationary orbit.

Polar satellite:- It  is a type of Earth-observing satellite that orbits the Earth, passing over or near the Earth's poles.

• It rotates in Polar plane.

• Its height from Earth surface is 500 km ~ 600 km.

• Its time period is 100 min.

• Used for weather data collection

Note: Any satellite is said to be in a condition of freely falling on Earth. (as only force acting on it is force

of gravity). Hence, apparent weight of any object in a satellite is always ZERO.

Orbital Velocity ($v_0$) :-

$\mathrm{v_0=\sqrt{\frac{GM_e}{r}}}$

Time period of orbital motion :-

$\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{r}}}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~T}^2 \propto \mathrm{r}^3$

Kinetic energy of satellite :-

$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{r}}$

Potential energy of satellite :-

$\mathrm{PE}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{r}}$

Total Mechanical Energy ($\mathrm{TE}$) :-

$\mathrm{TE}=-\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{r}}$

$\mathrm{KE}=-\mathrm{TE}=-\frac{\mathrm{PE}}{2}$

As total energy of a satellite is negative, it is called as bounded system.

Binding energy (BE = –TE)

$\mathrm{BE}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{r}}$

Work done to shift orbit of satellite :-

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {ext }}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{~m}}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)$
